thread.title: Markets Now: Dow Drops 149 Points as Turkey’s Pain Spreads

author: Ben Levisohn
title: Markets Now: Dow Drops 149 Points as Turkey’s Pain Spreads
text:
Markets Now: Dow Drops 227 Points as Support Holds…for Now August 15, 2018, 07:48:00 AM EDT By Ben Levisohn, Barron's
Want to know why the Dow Jones Industrial Average is doing what it's doing? Check back here for a semi-live look at the volatile markets from Barron's reporters. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg
11:57 a.m. 2800 held, and the S&P 500 was able to bounce a bit from there. The benchmark has fallen 1% to 2,812.27, well off its worst levels, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average has dropped 227.52 points, or 1%, to 25,072.40. The Nasdaq Composite has slumped 1.5% to 7,755.48.
Rick Bensignor , president of Bensignor Strategies , notes that 2800 has become a major support for the S&P 500, but he sees signs of "exhaustion" in the index that could mean a break is just a matter of time.
"It's no surprise that selling halted just north of 2800 today, as two prior lows held there recently, too," Bensignor writes. "But whether it happen today or in the next few days, any real break of 2800 will likely bring in more selling to bring us down to what we said was the pivotal number to watch right now, which is the bearish...level at 2778."
And if that breaks? Look for a test of the 200-day moving average, and perhaps a drop as far as 2693. Ouch.
Dow Drops 318 Points as Turkey, China Put Market to the Test
11:00 a.m. And it just gets worse. The S&P 500 has fallen 1.3% to 2804.37, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average has dropped 318.87 points, or 1.3%, to 24,981.05. The Nasdaq Composite has slumped 1.7% to 7736.05.
And it's just as ugly beneath the surface, with only utilities and real estate managing to rally, and consumer staples sitting near flat on the day. Oil stocks, in particular, are getting hit hard, withe the Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF ( XLE ) off 3.4% at $71.99 following higher crude oil inventories .
Keep an eye on 2800 in the S&P 500. It needs to hold, or this selloff could get much, much worse.
Dow Drops 282 Points as Turkey Might Just Be the Beginning
10:11 a.m. That escalated quickly. It looked like it would be just another run of the mill selloff, but instead, the market is really taking it on the chin.
The S&P 500 has fallen 1.1% to 2808.55, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average has dropped 282.50 points, or 1.1%, to 25,017.42. The Nasdaq Composite has slumped 1.4% to 7761.37.
Concerns around Turkey continue, despite the lira's 4.6% bounce, and other emerging markets are showing signs of strain as well. China, for instance, is seeing its stock market tumble following Tencent's ( TCEHY ) earnings and concerns around its debt market.
So is contagion brewing? Maybe not. Yes, emerging markets have a debt-to-GDP ratio of 37%, higher than it was in 1997, writes Wells Fargo economist Jay Bryson . But they're also in better position when it comes to paying off their debt. For starters, their currencies are now free floating; in the past they were fixed to the dollar. That means central banks can let currencies fall gradually and avoid having to raise interest rates to extremes, Bryson explains. He also points out that the ability to service the debt has also gotten better. "Vulnerable countries could experience their own external debt crises if their currencies continue to come under downward pressure and/or if the Fed hikes rates further," Bryson writes. "But we think that any other Turkey-like financial crises would be country specific rather than systemic à la 1997-1998."
Time will tell if he's right.
Dow Drops 149 Points as Turkey's Pain Spreads
7:30 a.m. Yesterday's rally proved to be just a respite from the crisis in Turkey , as stocks look set to sink this morning. S&P 500 futures have declined 0.5%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures have fallen 159 points, or 0.6%. Nasdaq Composite futures have dropped 0.7%.
Turkey placed tariffs on American goods , including alcohol, tobacco, and cars, and urged a boycott of Apple's ( AAPL ) iPhone. Turkey's lira continued to rally, but there were signs that the stress was spreading to other emerging markets, as Indonesia hiked its benchmark interest rate to support its currency. "Futures and most international markets traded lower overnight as contagion fears from Turkey's currency crisis persist despite further gains in the lira," writes The Sevens Report's Tom Essaye .
We won't get away that easily.
